    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/connectivetissuedisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Connective <span class="qt0">Tissue</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mixed Connective <span class="qt0">Tissue</span> Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PXE</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your connective <span class="qt0">tissue</span> supports many different parts of your body, such as your skin, eyes, and heart. It is like a "cellular glue" that gives your body parts their shape and helps keep them strong. It also helps some of your <span class="qt0">tissues</span> do their work. It is made of many kinds of proteins. Cartilage and fat are types of connective <span class="qt0">tissue</span>.</p><p>Over 200 disorders that impact connective <span class="qt0">tissue</span>. There are different types:</p><ul><li>Genetic disorders, such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and osteogenesis imperfecta</li><li>Autoimmune disorders, such as lupus and scleroderma</li><li>Cancers, like some types of soft <span class="qt0">tissue</span> sarcoma</li></ul><p>Each disorder has its own symptoms and needs different treatment.</p><p> NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/softtissuesarcoma.html">
      <content name="title">Soft <span class="qt0">Tissue</span> Sarcoma</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rhabdomyosarcoma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sarcoma, Soft <span class="qt0">Tissue</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your soft <span class="qt0">tissues</span> connect, support, or surround other <span class="qt0">tissues</span>. Examples include your muscles, tendons, fat, and blood vessels. Soft <span class="qt0">tissue</span> sarcoma is a cancer of these soft <span class="qt0">tissues</span>. There are many kinds, based on the type of <span class="qt0">tissue</span> they started in. They may cause a lump or swelling in the soft <span class="qt0">tissue</span>. Sometimes they spread and can press on nerves and organs, causing problems such as pain or trouble breathing.</p><p>No one knows exactly what causes these cancers. They are not common, but you have a higher risk if you have been exposed to certain chemicals, have had radiation therapy, or have certain genetic diseases.</p><p>Doctors diagnose soft <span class="qt0">tissue</span> sarcomas with a biopsy. Treatments include surgery to remove the tumor, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/organdonation.html">
      <content name="title">Organ Donation</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Donors</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Tissue</span> Donation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Organ donation takes healthy organs and <span class="qt0">tissues</span> from one person for transplantation into another. Experts say that the organs from one donor can save or help as many as 50 people. Organs you can donate include:</p><ul><li>Internal organs: Kidneys, heart, liver, pancreas, intestines, lungs </li><li>Skin </li><li>Bone and bone marrow </li><li>Cornea</li></ul><p>Most organ and <span class="qt0">tissue</span> donations occur after the donor has died. But some organs and <span class="qt0">tissues</span> can be donated while the donor is alive.</p><p>People of all ages and background can be organ donors. If you are under age 18, your parent or guardian must give you permission to become a donor. If you are 18 or older you can show you want to be a donor by signing a donor card. You should also let your family know your wishes.</p><p>Health Resources and Services Administration</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/endometriosis.html">
      <content name="title">Endometriosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Adenomyosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Endo</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is endometriosis?<p>The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. The uterus is lined with <span class="qt0">tissue</span> (endometrium). Endometriosis is a disease in which <span class="qt0">tissue</span> like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body. These patches of <span class="qt0">tissue</span> are called "implants," "nodules," or "lesions." They are most often found:</p><ul><li>On or under the ovaries</li><li>On the fallopian tubes, which carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus</li><li>Behind the uterus</li><li>On the <span class="qt0">tissues</span> that hold the uterus in place</li><li>On the bowels or bladder</li></ul><p>In rare cases, the <span class="qt0">tissue</span> may grow on your lungs or in other parts of your body.</p>What causes endometriosis?<p>Researchers don't know what causes endometriosis.</p>Who is at risk for endometriosis?<p>Endometriosis can affect anyone who menstruates. Certain factors can raise or lower your risk of getting it.</p><p>You are at higher risk if:</p><ul><li>You have a mother, sister, or daughter with endometriosis</li><li>Your period started before age 11</li><li>Your monthly cycles are short (less than 27 days)</li><li>Your menstrual cycles are heavy and last more than 7 days</li></ul><p>You have a lower risk if:</p><ul><li>You have been pregnant before</li><li>Your periods started late in adolescence</li><li>You breastfeed your babies</li></ul>What are the symptoms of endometriosis?<p>The main symptoms of endometriosis are:</p><ul><li>Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Infertility</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Painful menstrual cramps, which may get worse over time</li><li>Pain during or after sex</li><li>Pain in the intestine or lower abdomen</li><li>Pain with bowel movements (pooping) or urination (peeing), usually during your period</li><li>Heavy periods</li><li>Spotting or bleeding between periods</li><li>Digestive or gastrointestinal symptoms</li><li>Fatigue or lack of energy</li></ul>How is endometriosis diagnosed?<p>Surgery is the only way to know for sure that you have endometriosis. First, however, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. You will have a pelvic exam and may have some imaging tests.</p><p>The most common surgery to diagnose endometriosis is a laparoscopy. This is a type of surgery that uses a laparoscope, a thin tube with a camera and light. The surgeon inserts the laparoscope through a small cut in the skin near your belly button. Your provider can make a diagnosis based on how the patches of endometriosis look. They may also do a biopsy to get a <span class="qt0">tissue</span> sample.</p>What are the treatments for endometriosis?<p>There is no cure for endometriosis, but there are treatments for the symptoms. Your provider will work with you to decide which treatments would be best for you.</p><p>Treatments for endometriosis pain include:</p><ul><li>Pain relievers, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) such as ibuprofen and a prescription medicine specifically for endometriosis. Providers may sometimes prescribe opioids for severe pain.</li><li>Hormone therapy, which stops the ovaries from making hormones. This may slow the growth of the endometrial <span class="qt0">tissue</span> and may stop new areas from growing. Types of hormone therapy include: 
	<ul><li>Birth control pills.</li><li>Progestin therapy.</li><li>Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) medicines (GnRH agonists and antagonists).  These medicines cause a temporary menopause.  After your stop taking the medicines, your menstrual periods will start again, and pregnancy is possible.</li></ul></li><li>Surgical treatments for severe pain, including procedures to remove the endometriosis patches or cut some nerves in the pelvis. The surgery may be a laparoscopy or major surgery.</li></ul><p>Treatments for infertility caused by endometriosis include:</p><ul><li>Laparoscopy to remove the endometriosis patches</li><li>In vitro fertilization</li><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></ul></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/biopsy.html">
      <content name="title">Biopsy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A biopsy is a procedure that removes cells or <span class="qt0">tissue</span> from your body.  A doctor called a pathologist looks at the cells or <span class="qt0">tissue</span> under a microscope to check for damage or disease. The pathologist may also do other tests on it.</p><p>Biopsies can be done on all parts of the body. In most cases, a biopsy is the only test that can tell for sure if a suspicious area is cancer.  But biopsies are performed for many other reasons too.</p><p>There are different types of biopsies. A needle biopsy removes <span class="qt0">tissue</span> with a needle passed through your skin to the site of the problem. Other kinds of biopsies may require surgery.</p></content>
